# Identity and access management

This section shows you how to configure HCP Terraform or Terraform Enterprise to meet your requirements for delivering IaC services to your internal customers.

## Post-installation tasks

An optional step at the end of automated installation of Terraform Enterprise is the creation of the <a href="https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/enterprise/replicated/install/automated/automating-initial-user" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">Initial Admin Creation Token</a> (IACT), but further initialization tasks complete the setup. There are two viable options for post-provision configuration in Terraform Enterprise: API scripts or using the Terraform Provider. The best practice is to use the <a href="https://registry.terraform.io/providers/hashicorp/tfe/latest/docs" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">Terraform Enterprise provider</a> to derive state for the configuration.

## SSO and teams

The setup of SSO for HCP Terraform is not covered in detail in this document, as configurations can vary depending on the SAML 2.0-compliant provider used.

- You can find specific instructions for popular identity providers <a href="https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cloud-docs/users-teams-organizations/single-sign-on" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">here</a>.
- For applicable SAML 2.0 documentation, <a href="https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cloud-docs/users-teams-organizations/single-sign-on/saml" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">here</a>.

We recommend automating the creation of teams alongside projects, Stacks, and workspaces using the Terraform Enterprise provider. After creating the initial teams required, automate the addition of users within your strategic IdP platform. By adding a team attribute name (default: MemberOf) attribute within your IdP, you can automatically assign users to the created groups in the SAML configuration. You can find further details <a href="https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/enterprise/saml/configuration" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">here</a>.

Note: For user accounts used by pipelines, use `IsServiceAccount` set to true to flag these in SAML. See <a href="https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/enterprise/saml/attributes#isserviceaccount" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">`isserviceaccount`</a>. Create teams in Terraform Enterprise with the _exact_ name of the group in the IdP. Do not create users manually - Terraform Enterprise creates these automatically after it processes the SAML assertion at login.

### Team mapping with Microsoft Entra ID and Okta

Automated team mapping only works if the IdP actually emits the team attribute. Most SSO issues we see in the field are caused by a missing or misformatted `MemberOf` claim rather than by HCP Terraform or Terraform Enterprise. We recommend one of the following patterns with Microsoft Entra ID:

- **Group claim.** Add a group claim named `MemberOf` and set it to emit **Groups assigned to the application**. Other options such as **Security groups** can produce no usable values for the application. Entra ID emits group object IDs, so set each team's **SSO Team ID** to the object ID of the matching group and keep a human-readable team name.
- **App roles.** Add a claim named `MemberOf` with the value `user.assignedroles`. For each team, create an Entra ID group, create an app role in the enterprise application, assign the group to the role, and create a team named exactly after the role.

With either pattern:

- Team names and role names are matched literally and are case sensitive. Avoid spaces in team and role names.
- Teams are never created from the assertion. HCP Terraform and Terraform Enterprise ignore values that do not match an existing team, so create the team (with the `tfe` provider) before users sign in.
- Use a group naming prefix (for example `tfc-`) and filter the claim to groups with that prefix. This keeps the assertion small and makes the onboarding runbook repeatable: create the IdP group, create the team with the group ID, grant project access, and ask the user to sign in.
- Use a SAML tracing browser extension to inspect the assertion when a user lands in the wrong teams.

With Okta, configure the `MemberOf` attribute statement to send the team names. If a user's first SSO login presents an email address that does not match their existing account, link the SSO identity to the existing account instead of creating a new one, so you do not end up with duplicate accounts.

Identity providers without a dedicated HashiCorp guide, such as Keycloak, use the generic SAML configuration. Plan time for trial and error and secure access to the IdP administrators before the engagement starts; their availability is usually the critical path.

### User lifecycle and offboarding

The IdP only authenticates users. SAML SSO on its own does not deprovision accounts or remove organization membership:

- Removing or disabling a user in the IdP blocks new SSO sign-ins, but the user remains a member of the organization and their user API tokens are not deleted.
- To remove access immediately, also remove the user from the organization and revoke their tokens. Automate this with the `tfe` provider or the API as part of your offboarding process. In HCP Terraform, evaluate SCIM provisioning, which lets the IdP manage user and team lifecycle directly.
- Team membership is recalculated from the assertion each time a user signs in, so changes to IdP groups take effect at the next login, not immediately.
- In HCP Terraform, review the <a href="https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cloud-docs/users-teams-organizations/users#idle-session-timeout" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">idle session timeout</a> and forced re-authentication settings and reduce them to match your security policy. Set a maximum token expiration in the organization settings.
- In Terraform Enterprise, user API tokens are only accepted while the user's SAML session is valid; the site-wide **API Token Session Timeout** (default 14 days) controls this. Align it with your security policy. Refer to <a href="https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/enterprise/saml/login" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">API token expiration</a>.

<Note>

In HCP Terraform, account settings such as two-factor authentication and user API token generation are outside the scope of the organization's SSO configuration. Users are prompted to "step up" with their HCP Terraform or HCP credentials when they open these pages. This is expected behavior; tell users about it during onboarding.

</Note>

### Tokens for automation

Do not tie pipelines and automation to a person. We recommend creating dedicated teams with no members to act as service accounts: generate a <a href="https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cloud-docs/users-teams-organizations/api-tokens#team-api-tokens" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">team API token</a> for each and grant the team only the project or workspace access the automation needs. For example, use one team to create workspaces and queue runs, and a separate team that can only read state and write variables. Store team tokens in your secrets manager; Vault's <a href="https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/secrets/terraform" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">Terraform Cloud secrets engine</a> can generate and rotate organization, team, and user tokens.

## Connect to a version control system

We recommend connecting HCP Terraform/Terraform Enterprise to your VCS provider to enable workflows for managing modules in the private registry, managing Sentinel or OPA policy-sets, and connecting VCS-backed Stacks and workspaces to VCS repositories.

### GitHub app

If using GitHub, the preferred method of VCS connection is a GitHub App, for a number of reasons. A GitHub App is not tied to a specific user, does not require a personal access token, and is safe to set up as a static VCS connection with no need to rotate tokens. A GitHub App connects Terraform to GitHub, but confers no access permissions itself. Instead, the following elements  govern access to repositories.

- The GitHub organization(s) housing the GitHub App.
- Individual GitHub user permissions (to use the GitHub App, Terraform users must authorize it with their GitHub credentials).

See <a href="https://docs.github.com/en/apps/oauth-apps/building-oauth-apps/differences-between-github-apps-and-oauth-apps#about-github-apps-and-oauth-apps" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">GitHub's documentation</a> for more detail.

Terraform Enterprise supports a single site-wide GitHub App, shared across all Terraform Enterprise organizations. To use it, <a href="https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/enterprise/admin/application/github-app-integration" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">create and configure it</a> using a site administrator account.

Choose the appropriate level of visibility for your GitHub App from the following list.

- If you only have one GitHub organization, configure your GitHub App as private.
- If you have multiple organizations under the same GitHub Enterprise, <a href="https://docs.github.com/en/enterprise-cloud@latest/admin/managing-your-enterprise-account/creating-github-apps-for-your-enterprise" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">create the App under your enterprise account</a> (at the time of writing, this feature is in public preview).
- If you need access to repositories across multiple GitHub organizations, configure your GitHub App as public but do not list it on GitHub's marketplace.

HCP Terraform has a <a href="https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cloud-docs/vcs/github-app" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">pre-configured public GitHub app</a> which you can install in any GitHub organization(s) as required.

### OAuth

For providers other than GitHub, authorize VCS connections using OAuth within each Terraform Enterprise organization. Do this using a <a href="https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/enterprise/vcs" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">manual UI workflow</a> using an ID and secret from the VCS, or <a href="https://registry.terraform.io/providers/hashicorp/tfe/latest/docs/resources/oauth_client" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">automated using the HCP Terraform and Terraform Enterprise provider</a> using an access token from the respective VCS account. As with all static tokens, it is good practice to rotate this periodically.

OAuth authorizes Terraform Enterprise to act as a specific user or account on the VCS. The permissions of that account govern the access Terraform has to VCS organizations and repositories. For simplicity, we recommend setting up a single OAuth connection per VCS provider in each Terraform Enterprise organization. Use a service account with access to all IaC and policy-as-code repositories, to avoid any dependency on individual employee accounts.

If you require a more granular or least-privilege permissions model, you can create multiple OAuth VCS connections, each mapping a subset of VCS repositories to a subset of Terraform projects. In this case it would be a function of a landing-zone module to create these OAuth connections and <a href="https://registry.terraform.io/providers/hashicorp/tfe/latest/docs/resources/project_oauth_client" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">project mappings</a> on demand whenever a new project onboards.

Whichever method you choose, scope the connection's service account or GitHub App installation to the repositories that hold Terraform and policy code. When you install the GitHub App on selected repositories only, remember to grant each new Terraform or Sentinel repository explicitly. Complete the OAuth authorization in a single browser session on one workstation, signed in to the VCS as the service account; splitting the handshake between people or machines fails.

### Common VCS connectivity issues

VCS-driven workflows need connectivity in both directions: HCP Terraform or Terraform Enterprise must reach the VCS to clone code, and the VCS must reach HCP Terraform or Terraform Enterprise to deliver webhooks. Check both directions before you onboard teams. The following issues recur in the field:

- **Bitbucket Data Center (Terraform Enterprise):** Terraform Enterprise clones over SSH, so it needs the Bitbucket HTTP port (default 7990) and SSH port (default 7999), and the Terraform Enterprise CA bundle must trust Bitbucket's certificate. If Bitbucket rejects the SSH key generated during setup, regenerate it as an ECDSA key. In large Bitbucket estates, not every repository may appear in the repository list; enter the repository path manually, or use several service accounts each scoped to a smaller set of repositories.
- **GitLab self-managed (Terraform Enterprise):** If Terraform Enterprise uses a private address, GitLab blocks its webhooks until an administrator enables **Allow requests to the local network from webhooks and integrations**.
- **Azure DevOps (HCP Terraform):** Conditional access policies that require MFA block non-human access from HCP Terraform. Allowlist the <a href="https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cloud-docs/architectural-details/ip-ranges" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">HCP Terraform IP ranges</a> in your conditional access policy.
- **Self-hosted VCS with HCP Terraform:** The VCS must be reachable from the internet with a publicly trusted certificate and DNS that resolves externally. If that is not acceptable, use <a href="/validated-designs/terraform/administration-guide/self-hosted-agents#request-forwarding-hcp-terraform-only-premium-sku">request forwarding</a> through self-hosted agents.

## Audit

In HCP Terraform only, the <a href="https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cloud-docs/api-docs/audit-trails" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">Audit Trails API</a> provides access to audit events. We recommend Terraform Enterprise customers <a href="https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/enterprise/admin/infrastructure/logging" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">forward logs</a> for monitoring and auditing purposes. See the section on observability for more details.
Include audit, logging, and monitoring in the target architecture for the delivery of your project.  **Do not wait until after go-live to implement observability**.

## HCP Terraform agents

Pools of HCP Terraform agents allow HCP Terraform and Terraform Enterprise to communicate with isolated APIs in discrete network segments such as those on premise. We recommend defining agent pools and assigning Stacks and workspaces to them using the Terraform Enterprise provider as appropriate. This improves the availability of your on-premise APIs and allows for configuration of network hardware, internal VCS, CI/CD systems and so on, using IaC. This improves the return on investment of HCP Terraform and Terraform Enterprise.

You may choose to run multiple agents within your network, up to the organization's purchased agent limit (which only affects HCP Terraform customers; there is no such limit for Terraform Enterprise customers). Each agent process runs a single Terraform run at a time. Multiple agent processes can be concurrently run on a single instance, license limit permitting.

We strongly recommend reading the <a href="https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cloud-docs/agents" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">HCP Terraform agent documentation</a> as part of your implementation planning.

### Compatibility

Agents support Terraform versions 0.12 and later only. Workspaces configured to use Terraform versions below 0.12 cannot select the agent-based execution mode.

When running Terraform Enterprise, consult the <a href="https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/enterprise/releases" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">release notes</a> for agent version restrictions for your target Terraform Enterprise version and also the HashiCorp <a href="https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/enterprise/application-administration/agents-on-tfe" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">considerations for HCP Terraform agents on Terraform Enterprise</a>.

### Operational considerations

The agent runs in the foreground as a long-running process that continuously polls for workloads from HCP Terraform. An agent process may stop due to a variety of reasons. We strongly recommend pairing the agent with a process supervisor to ensure that it automatically restarts in case of an error. On a Linux host, do this using a `systemd` manifest such as the one below.

```
[Unit]
Description="HashiCorp HCP Terraform Agent"
Documentation="https://www.terraform.io/cloud-docs/agents"
Requires=network-online.target
After=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=Simple
User=tfcagent
Group=tfcagent
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/tfc-agent
KillMode=process
KillSignal=SIGINT
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5
EnvironmentFile=-/etc/sysconfig/tfc-agent

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

If using HCP Terraform agents in containers, use <a href="https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cloud-docs/agents/agents#optional-configuration-single-execution-mode" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">single-execution mode</a> to ensure your agent only runs a single workload and guarantees a clean working environment for every run.

### Upgrading HCP Terraform agents

When HashiCorp releases a new version of Terraform Enterprise, we test it against the most current HCP Terraform agent version. Should you need to upgrade your HCP Terraform agent version, we recommend testing the new version in a separate agent pool before rolling it out to your main agent pool(s). Use the platform team's dedicated HCP Terraform organization or Terraform Enterprise instance for this.

When considering use of HCP Terraform agents, do not skip testing, and we suggest that the extent of the testing effort must match the extent of the change. Patches and minor changes require little testing, while major changes require more extensive tests.
